senses.def: a commercial center with a number of places for doing business
senses.comment: ἀγορά differs in meaning from ἐμπόριον (57.206) in that the focus is upon a commercial center involving a number of places for doing business. The term ἐμπόριον may be used to refer to the same type of geographical location, but the focus is upon the activity and not the place.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to not being guilty of wrongdoing
the faculty of hearing
senses.comment: In some languages it may be better to speak about the organs involved rather than the related faculties, for example, ‘if the whole body were an eye, what about the ears?’

senses.def: (derivative of ἀκούω[a] ‘to hear,’ 24.52) that which is heard by someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of ‘message’ would be ‘that which is said’ rather than ‘that which is heard,’ and accordingly, one may perhaps best translate Romans 10:16 as ‘who has believed what we said.’

senses.def: (derivative of ἀκούω[c] ‘to receive news,’ 33.212) the content of the news which is heard
senses.comment: In a number of languages, however, it is impossible to speak of ‘news spreading.’ It therefore may be necessary to render Matthew 4:24 as ‘people throughout the whole country of Syria kept hearing from one another about him.’

senses.def: to believe something and to respond to it on the basis of having heard
(a Semitic idiom, literally: to hear with hearing) to listen intently and with presumed continuity
(an idiom, literally: to itch with respect to hearing) to have one’s ears tickled by what is heard
glosses: to desire to hear what one wants to hear

senses.def: pertaining to no longer experiencing sorrow or anxiety
to provide information, with the possible implication of considerable detail
to leap or spring up, presumably from a seated position

senses.comment: The occurrence of ἀνθρακιά ‘charcoal fire’ in John 18:18 fits the context well, since a charcoal fire provides a maximum of heat with a minimum of smoke. The making and use of charcoal is widespread throughout the world, and there is generally no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘charcoal.’ However, where such a term does not exist, it is possible to speak of ‘a wood fire’ or simply ‘a fire.’

senses.def: pertaining to being unable to be controlled by something or someone
senses.comment: It is possible to restructure this statement in Hebrews 2:8 so as to read ‘God left nothing that man could not be in control of.’ It is also possible to translate this expression as ‘and God put him in control over all things.’

senses.def: (derivative of ὑποτάσσομαι ‘to obey,’ 36.18) pertaining to being rebelliously disobedient
pertaining to willing and generous giving
to be in perplexity, with the implication of serious anxiety

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: behavior completely lacking in moral restraint, usually with the implication of sexual licentiousness
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘licentious behavior’ would be ‘to live like a dog’ or ‘to act like a goat’ or ‘to be a rooster,’ in each instance pertaining to promiscuous sexual behavior.

senses.def: pertaining to being willing, with the implication of choice
the husks of grain
senses.comment: Chaff may be referred to in some languages as ‘the empty part of the grain’ or ‘the leaves of the grain’ or ‘the refuse of the grain.’

senses.def: thin straight rod with a sharp point; may be propelled by a bow (arrow) or by hand (dart); used as a weapon in hunting or battle
senses.comment: In the NT βέλος occurs only in a highly figurative context: τὰ βέλη … πεπυρωμένα flaming arrows (or darts) Ephesians 6:16, referring to temptations by the Devil.

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: to think, with the purpose of planning or deciding on a course of action
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are two quite distinct sets of terms for planning depending upon the purpose involved in such planning. If the planning is constructive, either for oneself or someone else, one set of terms is likely to be used, while if the planning is harmful (usually against someone else), another set of terms would be used.|This meaning is also found as a variant reading: Οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες διεπρίοντο καὶ ἐβούλοντο ἀνελεῖν αὐτούς ‘but when they heard this they were furious, for they were planning to put them to death’ Acts 5:33 (apparatus).

senses.def: to think over carefully in an attempt to make a decision

senses.comment: A number of languages distinguish clearly between various types of laughter: (1) laughter directed against some person as a form of ridicule; (2) laughter resulting from seeing some humorous event or as the result of listening to a humorous account; and (3) laughter which reflects happiness and joy. In Luke 6:21 and James 4:9 it is this third type of laughter which is relevant to the contexts.

senses.def: the state of being naked or only scantily clothed
senses.comment: In the context of Romans 8:35 ‘nakedness’ refers to poverty.

senses.def: to strike or beat repeatedly
to be reconciled to someone
the tax required of every male Jew from the age of twenty onward; to support the temple
senses.comment: The two-drachma coin referred to in Matthew 17:24 was approximately equivalent to two denarii. The meaning of δίδραχμον is treated here in Domain 57 rather than in Domain 6 (where the value of other coins is discussed) since the focus of the meaning of δίδραχμον is the required Temple tax rather than the value or form of the coin itself.

senses.def: to try to learn the genuineness of something by examination and testing, often through actual use
glosses: to try to determine the genuineness of

senses.def: genuineness on the basis of having been tested
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to freedom from anxiety and inner turmoil
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκκρέμαμαι ‘to hang out from,’ not occurring in the NT) to pay unusually close attention to what is being said
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐκκρέμαμαι in Luke 19:48, see 68.15.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκκρέμαμαι ‘to hang from,’ not occurring in the NT) to persist in doing something
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐκκρέμαμαι in Luke 19:48, see 30.34.

senses.def: pertaining to being relatively light in weight
senses.comment: Though in Matthew 11:30 ἐλαφρός can be understood in a literal sense, the entire statement in this verse is, of course, figurative. Therefore, one can also interpret ἐλαφρός in Matthew 11:30 as figurative (see 22.38). Note, however, that the phrase ὁ … ζυγός μου does not refer to something which Christ carries but to something which he places upon his followers. The same is true of the phrase τὸ φορτίον μου ‘my burden,’ which is the burden he gives to his disciples or servants.

senses.def: a strictly limited point on the lower part of a scale of extent
pertaining to that which is easy to bear or endure
senses.comment: It is possible to render ἐλαφρός in Matthew 11:30 as ‘light,’ in the sense of ‘light in weight’ (see 86.2). However, if ‘burden’ in Matthew 11:30 is understood figuratively, ἐλαφρός can generally also be understood in a figurative sense.

senses.def: fashionable braiding (of the hair)
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is possible to employ as an equivalent of ἐμπλοκῆς τριχῶν in 1 Peter 3:3 ‘elaborate hairdo’ or ‘fancy way in which the hair is combed.’

senses.def: (derivative of νόμος[a] ‘law, rule,’ 33.333) pertaining to being in accordance with law
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘legal meeting’ would be ‘regular meeting’ or ‘a meeting called by an official’ or ‘a meeting authorized by an official.’

senses.def: pertaining to being under obligation imposed by law
senses.comment: In some languages there is a difficulty involved in rendering ἔννομος by a phrase such as ‘under law,’ since this may be understood in a sense of ‘beneath the law’ or ‘illegal.’ A more common expression would be ‘tied to the law’ or ‘obligated by the law.’

senses.subdomain: Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
senses.def: a day immediately following a previous day
the process of causing something to begin

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: (derivative of ἐπιμελέομαι[b] ‘to think about,’ 30.40) pertaining to the manner of giving thoughtful concern to an activity
to make available whatever is necessary to help or supply the needs of someone
to provide something in addition to what already exists
ancestor of the human race
a state of beauty or fine appearance, with the implication of being attractive and well-suited
to bring under control and to continue to restrain
senses.comment: In many languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘bringing a person under control.’ It may therefore be more appropriate to use some such phrase as ‘not allow a person to do just what he wants’ or ‘make a person behave’ or ‘make a person obey.’ In speaking of animals, one may render James 3:7 as ‘all kinds of wild animals … can be made to obey a person.’

senses.def: to have confidence and firmness of purpose in the face of danger or testing
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘courage’ is rendered by an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to not move,’ ‘to be deaf to threats,’ and ‘to have a heart like iron.’

senses.def: appropriate beliefs and devout practice of obligations relating to supernatural persons and powers
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no specific term equivalent to ‘religion,’ but one may always speak of this phase of culture by some phrase such as ‘how to act toward God’ or ‘what one does to placate spirits’ or ‘how one worships.’

senses.def: a king of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a reference to an entity regarded as relatively absent in terms of the discourse setting
to gain complete victory over, as the result of a strenuous struggle
to cause to cease to exist
glosses: to cause to come to an end

senses.def: to cause to cease to happen
to render ineffective the power or force of something
senses.comment: In rendering this expression in 1 Corinthians 1:28 it may be quite necessary to stipulate the reference to τὰ ὄντα, and in this context the contrast between τὰ ὄντα and τὰ μὴ ὄντα may perhaps be best expressed as ‘those things that are not regarded as important in order to abolish those that are regarded as important.’ The rendering of these expressions depends, of course, upon the manner in which the preceding context from verse 26 is rendered.

senses.def: to cause the release from an association with a person or an institution on the basis that the earlier obligation or restriction is no longer relevant or in force
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of being freed from a law which stipulates the relationship a woman has to her husband. Accordingly, it may be appropriate to translate this statement in Romans 7:2 as ‘if a woman’s husband dies, the law no longer ties her to her husband’ or even ‘… the law says she is free to marry someone else.’

senses.def: to cease to happen
pertaining to being in a position below a point of orientation
senses.comment: See discussion at 1.18.

senses.def: the father of King Saul
movement through water by the use of limbs
senses.comment: A number of languages have several different terms for ‘swim’ depending on whether it is a person, an animal, a fish, or an eel (or a snake). Care must be exercised in choosing the appropriate term for this context.

senses.def: one who presides over a court session and pronounces judgment
the father of Noah in the genealogy of Jesus
a Roman pound, weighing about twelve ounces or about 325 grams
senses.comment: In speaking of perfume in John 12:3 it may be far better to indicate quantity rather than weight, and therefore one may translate ‘then Mary took a pint of perfume.’ In translating λίτρα in the NT, one need not identify the pound as being ‘a Roman pound.’ It is better to employ a common term for pound (normally weighing sixteen ounces) or to provide a rounded-off equivalent of the amount in metric units, for example, three hundred grams or one-half liter.

senses.def: to think or reason in a completely irrational manner
glosses: to not be in one’s right mind
to be out of one’s mind

senses.def: the upper range of a scale of extent, with the possible implication of importance in relevant contexts
senses.comment: In Ephesians 1:19 there are two expressions of degree, ὑπερβάλλον (treated in 78.33) and μέγεθος, which, though syntactically the head of the phrase, is semantically an expression of degree with δύναμις[b] ‘power’ (76.1).

senses.def: a position defined by the location of two objects, one on each side
a marker of an exclusive association

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is subsequent in order to a previous point of time
a Christian from Cyprus
an affirmative response to questions or statements or an emphatic affirmation of a statement
a person who is skilled in the teaching and interpretation of the law (in the NT referring to the law of the OT)
a servant in a household
act of expressing openly one’s allegiance to a proposition or person
senses.comment: It is often extremely difficult, if not impossible, to translate ὁμολογέω[a], ὁμολογία, and ἐξομολογέω[b] by the usual expression for ‘confess,’ since this would usually imply that one has done something wrong. It is normally necessary, therefore, to employ quite a different type of relationship, usually involving a public utterance and an expression of confidence or allegiance. For example, in Matthew 10:32 it may be necessary to translate ‘whoever tells people publicly that he is loyal to me, I will tell my Father that I am loyal to that person.’ Similarly, in Hebrews 10:23 one may translate ‘let us hold on to the hope in which we have told people we have such confidence.’ Likewise, in Romans 15:9 one may translate ‘therefore I will tell the Gentiles how I have put my confidence in you.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of a term meaning literally ‘to hunt,’ ‘to trap,’ not occurring in the NT) to acquire information about an error or fault, with the purpose of causing harm or trouble
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is possible to retain the figurative meaning of ‘trap’ or ‘catch,’ but in a number of instances other figures are used, for example, ‘to cause to trip,’ ‘to cause to fall,’ ‘to hear wrong words from his mouth,’ or ‘to use his words against him.’

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to sit down near or beside someone
the state of a person who has not had sexual intercourse (in the NT referring only to females; compare 9.33 and 9.39)
senses.comment: See also discussion at 9.39.

senses.def: the father of one’s spouse
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must indicate explicitly the various components of meaning in ‘father-in-law.’ For example, πενθερός in John 18:13 may be rendered as ‘Caiaphas had married the daughter of Annas’ or ‘the daughter of Annas had become the wife of Caiaphas.’

senses.def: Asiatic Rock dove: bird with a blue-gray color with a pinkish sheen to the neck feathers and a black tip on its tail; lives in large colonies and eats mainly seeds; courts, mates, and has nests several times a year; nests on rock ledges; Columba via; used as food and for sacrifices; regarded as swift, docile, and innocent
senses.comment: Though in English a relatively clear distinction is made between ‘doves’ (which have pointed tails) and ‘pigeons’ (which have square off tails), there seems to be no such distinction in the use of περιστερά and τρυγών in the Greek of the New Testament.|There are, however, certain problems involved in the connotations of terms relating to pigeons or doves. According to ancient zoology, the dove was thought to have no bile, and consequently, therefore, to be a very peaceful and clean bird. It thus became a symbol of Christian virtue and of gentleness (as in Matthew 10:16). In reality, however, doves and pigeons are quite aggressive, and a group of pigeons are frequently known to peck an injured bird to death. Therefore, in some societies pigeons or doves are not regarded as gentle or peaceful, but rather as wicked and harmful. In fact, in some cultures doves are thought to be symbols of death and of evil. Under such circumstances it is important, therefore, to have some marginal note so as to indicate clearly the symbolic significance of such birds in biblical contexts.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to take advantage of someone, usually as the result of a motivation of greed
pertaining to that which occurs in many kinds of ways
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πολυτρόπως in Hebrews 1:1, see 89.82.

senses.def: pertaining to occurring in many ways or manners
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πολυτρόπως in Hebrews 1:1, see 58.29.

senses.def: to go prior to someone else’s going
to move in front of or ahead of, with the implication that both parties are moving in the same direction
to lead or bring forward or forth
glosses: to bring forward to lead forth

senses.def: to happen or occur previous to some point of time
to go beyond established bounds of teaching or instruction, with the implication of failure to obey properly
the right or opportunity to address someone, implying higher status of the person addressed
to address an audience, with possible emphasis upon loudness
to call out, with the probable implication of seeking some response
to call to, with a possible implication of a reciprocal relation
a pile or heap of burning material
senses.comment: The Greek phrase ἅψαντες … πυράν ‘to kindle a fire’ is best rendered in a number of languages by a single verb meaning ‘to make a fire,’ and in some languages it is strange to speak of a ‘fire’ without indicating the type of material which is being burned. Hence, in Acts 28:2 the appropriate equivalent would be ‘they caused some sticks to burn.’|In some languages a very important distinction is made between two functionally different kinds of fire, one used for getting rid of refuse and the other used for warming oneself. Fire as a destructive agent, mentioned frequently in the book of Revelation (Revelation 8:5 and Revelation 20:10), may require quite a different term from what is used in speaking of a fire for the purpose of warming a person or heating an object.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of moral impurity and filth
a Jewish festival commemorating God’s provision during the wanderings in the wilderness
senses.comment: In some languages it may be useful to speak of the Festival of Tents as ‘the festival when people lived in tents.’

senses.def: the residue from a burned substance
senses.comment: It may be important in rendering σποδὸς δαμάλεως to indicate that the ashes are the result of the animal having been burned as a sacrifice, for example, ‘the ashes of a heifer burned as a sacrifice.’ Otherwise, the relationship between ‘ashes’ and ‘heifer’ may be difficult, if not impossible, for readers to understand.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to live sensually by gratifying the senses with sexual immorality
one form of the apostle Peter’s Aramaic name
a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
an elderly man of Jerusalem (Luke 2:25)
a Christian prophet at Antioch who was also called Niger
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
one who is a fellow slave or a slave alongside another slave
senses.comment: In some languages there is a very strong negative connotation in any word meaning ‘slave,’ for it may suggest ‘vile person’ or even ‘foreigner,’ since in a number of areas only foreigners were made slaves. It may therefore be necessary to use a term for slave which is more or less equivalent to ‘servant,’ ‘one who works without pay,’ ‘one who must work without pay,’ or ‘bondservant.’

senses.def: a sign which has been previously agreed upon as having a particular meaning or significance
senses.comment: If a language has no specific term for ‘signal’ or ‘sign,’ one may indicate the implications of σύσσημον by translating the first part of Mark 14:44 as follows: ‘the one who betrayed him told them how he would indicate who Jesus was; he said, The one whom I kiss is the man.’

senses.def: to put or place in a particular location

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
to remove or take off clothing
to explain something, presumably by putting forward additional or different information
to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest
to cause a state to be
to cause someone to experience, with the implication of subjecting a person to something
(an idiom, literally: to put a plan) to suggest a plan of action
(an idiom, literally: to put into the ears) to listen carefully to, with the implication of not forgetting
senses.comment: For another interpretation of this idiom in Luke 9:44, see 29.5.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to place in the ears) to continue to bear something in mind
senses.comment: For another interpretation of the idiom τίθεμαι εἰς τὰ ὦτα in Luke 9:44, see 24.64.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to place in the heart) to store information in the mind, with the implication of its being valuable
glosses: to treasure up in the heart
to store in the mind as valuable

senses.def: (idioms, literally: to place in the heart, and: to place in the mind) to engage in the process of deciding
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret the phrase ἐν τῷ πνεύματι in Acts 19:21 as being a reference to the Holy Spirit and accordingly, the passage may be translated as ‘Paul, led by the Spirit, decided to travel through Macedonia.’

senses.def: (idioms, literally: to put at someone’s feet) to present something to someone who is reckoned as having superior status or position

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to place the knees, a Latinism) to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
senses.comment: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to lay down one’s life) to die, with the implication of voluntary or willing action
senses.comment: Though in English the phrases ‘to lay down one’s life’ or ‘to give one’s life’ do suggest a voluntary dying, a literal rendering of such expressions in other languages would not necessarily imply the same. It may therefore be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to die willingly’ or ‘to die without resisting.’ In some languages ‘willingly’ is expressed primarily as a negation of objecting, for example, ‘I will not object to dying.’

senses.def: a Christian of Ephesus and companion of Paul
(with the genitive) a marker of a participant who is benefited by an event or on whose behalf an event takes place
senses.comment: In a number of languages, one cannot speak of ‘doing something on behalf of sins’; only a person can be benefited by an event, and therefore one must translate ‘who gave himself on behalf of us who had sinned’ in Galatians 1:4. See also 90.39.

senses.def: (with the genitive) a marker of general content, whether of a discourse or mental activity
a degree which is beyond that of a compared scale of extent

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a marker of status which is superior to another status
a marker of cause or reason, often with the implication of something which has been beneficial
to hold oneself back from doing something, with the implication of some fearful concern
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὑποστέλλω in Acts 20:27, see 68.53.

senses.def: to cease doing something of presumed positive value because of adverse circumstances or fear
senses.comment: It is also possible to translate this clause in Galatians 2:12 as ‘he withdrew and separated himself.’ For another interpretation of ὑποστέλλω in Acts 20:27, see 13.160.

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to the latter part of autumn
senses.comment: The use of φθινοπωρινός in Jude 1:12 should not be understood to imply that the fruit has already been picked, but rather that the trees in question have not produced fruit at all, and even in late autumn there is no productivity.

senses.def: to explain the meaning of something, with the implication that the text in question is difficult or complex
to give or grant graciously and generously, with the implication of good will on the part of the giver
to forgive, on the basis of one’s gracious attitude toward an individual
senses.comment: It may be useful in some instances to translate χαρίζομαι in 2 Corinthians 12:13 as ‘be so kind as to forgive me.’

senses.def: to release a person from the obligation of repaying what is owed
to hand someone over into the control of another person, without some reasonable cause
glosses: to put into the control of someone

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: an indefinite unit of time (the actual extent of time being determined by the context)

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: points of time consisting of occasions for particular events
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no general term for ‘time’ or ‘occasion.’ In some contexts it is simply not necessary to have such a term. For example, in rendering Matthew 13:30 one may translate ‘when the harvest comes, I will say to the reapers’ or ‘when people begin to harvest, I will say to the reapers.’ In other contexts, a term which normally refers to some unit is employed in a generic sense, as in the case of Greek ὥρα which means literally ‘hour’ but is frequently used as a generic expression for a point of time, as in Matthew 8:13. In Acts 7:17 χρόνος may often be rendered by a generic expression such as ‘day,’ for example, ‘when it was almost the day for God to keep his promise.’ In the case of Matthew 26:45, the nearness of the time may be indicated as ‘very soon the Son of Man will be handed over.’|Though it seems quite ordinary in English for one to speak of ‘time coming’ or ‘… drawing near,’ this type of figurative usage is impossible in many languages. The equivalent may be simply ‘will soon be’ or ‘is about to happen.’ The expression οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου (literally ‘my time has not yet come’) in John 2:4 denotes that it is not yet the occasion for a particular event (see καιρός in John 7:8 and compare John 7:10) but that it will soon be. In these contexts the expression may be rendered as ‘there is still time’ or ‘I will soon do it.’ In John 7:30 and John 8:20 (οὔπω ἐληλύθει ἡ ὥρα αὐτοῦ ‘his time has not yet come’) the reference is to the occasion of his eventual arrest, implying that it will indeed happen.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: an exceedingly long period of time from an assumed beginning up to the present
a relatively weak marker of a relationship between events or states
a degree which approximates a point on a scale of extent, either above or below
